concepts: CapEx vs OpEx: the cloud's consumption model shifts IT spend from upfront capital purchases to pay-as-you-go operational expense — idle on-premises capacity is money already spent.
Deployment models: public cloud is provider-managed and multi-tenant; private cloud is dedicated; hybrid keeps sensitive workloads local while bursting to the public cloud.

Regions, availability zones, and region pairs: a region is a set of datacenters; zones are isolated datacenters within a region for in-region resilience; region pairs give a recovery target at least 300 miles away.
Management hierarchy: management groups sit above subscriptions, which sit above resource groups, which hold resources. Policies and RBAC assigned higher up inherit downward — govern once at the top.
Pricing tools: the Pricing Calculator estimates a service bill; the TCO Calculator builds the migration business case against on-premises costs; Cost Management tracks actual spend after migration.
SLAs: every service publishes an uptime SLA. The composite SLA for serial dependencies is the product of the individual SLAs — every dependency lowers the total, so minimize the critical path.

example.code:
az account list --output table      # subscriptions you can deploy into
az group create -n ilb-prod -l eastus  # lifecycle boundary for the workload
example.walkthrough: A subscription is the billing and access boundary; a resource group is the lifecycle boundary inside it. Create the group once, deploy into it, and deleting the group later removes everything it holds — cleanup as one deliberate action.

pitfalls: Common trap: availability sets and availability zones are the same thing — sets protect within one datacenter (fault/update domains); zones are separate datacenters.
Common trap: the Pricing Calculator and the TCO Calculator are interchangeable — one estimates a bill, the other compares migration against on-premises.
Common trap: composite SLA is the average of the services — it is the product, and the chain is weaker than any single link.
Common trap: resource groups enforce naming or access — they organize and lifecycle-manage; Policy enforces rules and RBAC grants access.
lessons.title: AZ-900: Azure Fundamentals — Core concepts
lessons.try_it: Run the Azure CLI missions in the Terminal tab →

concepts: Machine learning learns patterns from data. Supervised learning trains on labeled examples (classification predicts categories, regression predicts numbers); unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data.
Azure AI services are pretrained models exposed as APIs — Vision for images, Language for text, Speech for audio — so you get AI capabilities without training data or ML expertise.
Generative AI creates new content (text, images, code) from prompts. It predicts plausible output, which is why every output must be verified, never trusted blindly.
Conversational AI combines a bot framework with language understanding: intents (what the user wants) and entities (the details) drive the dialog and decide when to escalate to a human.
Responsible AI: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability. Test models for bias, and disclose AI use to the people it affects.

example.walkthrough: The pretrained Vision model returns detected objects with confidence scores — no training step, no labeled dataset. Your job is deciding what to do with a 0.98-confidence apple versus a 0.51-confidence one: thresholds are a business decision, not a model detail.

pitfalls: Common trap: AI, ML, and deep learning are synonyms — AI is the field, ML learns from data, deep learning is ML with neural networks.
Common trap: classification and regression are interchangeable — classification predicts categories, regression predicts numbers.
Common trap: a pretrained model needs your training data to work — it works out of the box; fine-tuning is optional.
Common trap: generative AI output is factual — it generates plausible text, not verified facts.
lessons.title: AI-900: Azure AI Fundamentals — Core concepts
lessons.try_it: List the AI services in the Terminal tab →

concepts: Relational data lives in tables with fixed schemas and relationships; non-relational (NoSQL) trades the fixed schema for flexible document, key-value, graph, or column-family shapes.
OLTP systems process many small transactions (checkout); OLAP systems run heavy analytical queries over history (quarterly reports). Opposite access patterns — different services.
Batch processing handles data at rest on a schedule; stream processing handles data in motion in near real time — fraud detection cannot wait for the nightly job.
A data lake stores raw data in native format; a data warehouse stores structured, refined data for analytics. A lakehouse combines both.
ETL transforms before loading (schema-on-write); ELT loads first and transforms in the target (schema-on-read). The choice follows where compute is cheapest.
Azure data services: SQL Database (relational), Cosmos DB (globally distributed NoSQL), Synapse Analytics (warehouse-scale analytics), Data Factory (pipelines), Power BI (visualization).

example.code: orders (OLTP) → Data Factory pipeline → Synapse (OLAP) → Power BI dashboard
example.walkthrough: Transactional orders flow through an ELT pipeline into the warehouse, where analytical queries aggregate them without touching the checkout database. Each service does the job it was built for — that separation is the whole point.

pitfalls: Common trap: one database serves every workload — OLTP and OLAP have opposing access patterns and belong on different services.
Common trap: a data lake and a data warehouse are the same — the lake holds raw native data; the warehouse holds structured, query-ready data.
Common trap: Cosmos DB is just another relational database — it is multi-model NoSQL with global distribution.
Common trap: streaming is just faster batch — it processes each event as it arrives, enabling real-time decisions.
lessons.title: DP-900: Azure Data Fundamentals — Core concepts
lessons.try_it: Inventory the data services in the Terminal tab →

concepts: Zero Trust: never trust, always verify. Assume breach, verify explicitly with identity and device signals, and grant least-privilege access per request — trust is earned, never inherited from the network.
Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity provider: single sign-on, multifactor authentication, and Conditional Access policies that gate each sign-in by risk (location, device, behavior).
Defense in depth stacks controls across layers — physical, identity and access, network, compute, application, data — so no single failure exposes everything.
Microsoft Defender for Cloud gives a secure score with posture recommendations; Defender XDR correlates signals across endpoints, identity, email, and apps into incidents.
Shared responsibility: Microsoft secures the cloud platform; you secure your data, identities, and configurations — classification, access control, and encryption decisions stay yours.
Compliance: Purview tracks data governance and regulatory compliance with a compliance score; Azure Policy enforces resource rules at scale; both answer the auditor.

example.code: Sign-in from new country → Conditional Access → require MFA → device compliant? → allow / deny
example.walkthrough: Zero Trust in one flow: every sign-in is evaluated against policy — identity, location, device health — before access is granted. A report-only policy protects no one; enforcement is the difference.

pitfalls: Common trap: a firewall alone equals Zero Trust — Zero Trust is identity-centric and per-request, not a perimeter.
Common trap: the secure score and the compliance score measure the same thing — secure score is security posture (Defender); compliance score is regulatory posture (Purview).
Common trap: MFA means passwords do not matter — weak passwords plus push fatigue still get breached; prefer phishing-resistant methods.
Common trap: encryption is Microsoft's job entirely — you own your data's classification, access, and key decisions.

msf-ai-conversational.hint: What two jobs must the bot do — talk, and understand?
msf-ai-conversational.prompt: Which Azure AI building blocks fit?
msf-ai-conversational.situation: A university wants its website to answer common questions — deadlines, enrollment steps — at 2 AM, and escalate to staff whenever the bot is unsure.
msf-ai-conversational.title: The after-hours helpdesk
msf-ai-conversational.why: Conversational AI pairs a bot framework (Bot Service: channels, dialog flow, escalation) with language understanding (intent classification, entity extraction) so the bot knows what the user wants. Search retrieves documents but does not converse; training a foundation model from scratch is orders of magnitude beyond a fundamentals-level FAQ bot.

choices: Use a pretrained Azure AI Vision model for object detection — no training data required
Train a custom model in Azure Machine Learning from scratch
Use Azure AI Speech to transcribe shelf audio
Build the detector on top of Azure AI Search indexes
msf-ai-vision.hint: Do they need to teach a model from zero, or can they borrow one that has already learned?
msf-ai-vision.situation: A grocery chain photographs every store shelf nightly and wants to flag empty slots and count products automatically. There is no ML team, no labeled training data, and the pilot must launch in weeks.
msf-ai-vision.title: The shelf-scan audit
msf-ai-vision.why: Pretrained vision models (image analysis, object detection) are built for exactly this: point them at images and get labeled objects back with confidence scores, no training data or ML expertise needed. Custom training is the fallback for unusual domains, not the starting point; Speech and Search solve different problems.

choices: Analytical workload on Azure Synapse Analytics, visualized in Power BI
Run the aggregates on the production Azure SQL Database
Query Azure Cosmos DB for the historical rollups
Export everything to Blob Storage and read it manually
msf-analytics-report.hint: Is this asking the database to take orders, or to remember them?
msf-analytics-report.prompt: Which workload and service combination fits?
msf-analytics-report.situation: Executives want a weekly dashboard over three years of sales history — terabytes of data, aggregated by region and product, refreshed every Monday morning.
msf-analytics-report.title: The Monday dashboard
msf-analytics-report.why: This is an analytical (OLAP) workload: heavy reads over historical data for reporting. Synapse Analytics is built for that scale, and Power BI turns the results into dashboards. Running it on the transactional database risks slowing checkout; Cosmos DB serves operational, not analytical, queries.

choices: Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager — tracks controls and produces a compliance score
Defender for Cloud secure score — that measures security posture, not compliance
Azure Policy alone — it enforces rules but does not score a compliance program
A shared spreadsheet of screenshots
msf-compliance-purview.hint: Which tool speaks the auditor's language — controls and scores?
msf-compliance-purview.situation: A regulator asks a healthcare company to prove its data-handling controls and show its compliance posture improving quarter over quarter.
msf-compliance-purview.title: The audit letter
msf-compliance-purview.why: Compliance Manager assesses your Microsoft 365 data against regulations and standards, scores your compliance posture, and recommends improvement actions — exactly what an auditor wants to see trending upward. Defender for Cloud's secure score measures security posture; Azure Policy enforces resource rules; spreadsheets do not scale.

choices: Azure Cosmos DB — globally distributed, multi-model, low-latency reads and writes
Azure SQL Database — relational, regional by default
Azure Blob Storage — object storage, not low-latency transactional
Azure Synapse Analytics — built for analytics, not operational transactions
msf-cosmos-db.hint: Which service promises the cart is fast everywhere, not just in one region?
msf-cosmos-db.prompt: Which Azure data service is built for this?
msf-cosmos-db.situation: An e-commerce company needs shopping carts readable and writable with single-digit-millisecond latency from every continent, with JSON documents as the data shape.
msf-cosmos-db.title: The cart that follows you
msf-cosmos-db.why: Cosmos DB is the globally distributed database: data replicates to any Azure region with guaranteed low-latency reads and writes, and it stores document, key-value, graph, and column-family shapes. SQL Database is relational and regional by default; Blob is object storage; Synapse serves analytics workloads.

choices: Microsoft Entra ID with multifactor authentication and Conditional Access policies
On-premises Active Directory alone with no cloud sync
One shared admin password rotated monthly
A VPN as the only access control
msf-entra-id.hint: What checks the person, not just the network?
msf-entra-id.situation: A firm onboards fifty contractors who need access to cloud apps from personal devices. IT wants phishing-resistant sign-in and policies that block logins from unusual locations.
msf-entra-id.title: The contractor's laptop
msf-entra-id.why: Entra ID is the cloud identity provider: MFA adds a second factor beyond passwords, and Conditional Access enforces policies — require MFA, block risky locations — before granting access to apps. On-premises AD alone cannot gate cloud apps; shared passwords destroy accountability; a VPN encrypts traffic but does not verify identity per app.

simulations.brief: A company is moving 40 VMs to Azure over one quarter. Finance wants a cost case, the CISO wants guardrails, and the app team wants no downtime. Work the migration in the right order.
simulations.debrief: You ran the cloud adoption sequence: cost case first, governance before resources, resilience by design.

evidence:
Subject: Azure migration — need the 3-year cost case by Friday.
We cannot approve a hardware refresh AND cloud spend.
steps.explain: The TCO Calculator builds the migration business case: current on-premises costs versus projected Azure spend. Buying reservations or deploying before the estimate locks you into numbers you never validated.
options: Run the TCO Calculator comparison before anything else
Deploy the VMs now and measure the bill later
Buy 3-year reserved capacity today to lock the price
Ask each team to estimate their own costs in spreadsheets
steps.symptom: The CFO asks: what will this cost over three years versus refreshing the datacenter?

evidence:
ops-lead: we can add policy later, let's just move fast
meijia: do we have any guardrails yet?
steps.explain: Governance lands before resources: hierarchy (management groups), standards (naming, tags), and guardrails (Policy, locks). Move-fast-and-govern-later is how surprise bills and exposed resources happen.
options: Define management groups, naming/tagging standards, and Azure Policy guardrails first
Hand out Contributor on the subscription to all fifty engineers
Deploy now, govern later
Create one resource group and let everyone share it
steps.symptom: The cost case is approved. Fifty engineers start deploying into the subscription on Monday.

evidence:
Web tier: 4 VMs, single datacenter, session state in memory.
Requirement: survive one datacenter failure.
steps.explain: Availability zones are separate datacenters within the region — spreading the tier across zones survives a datacenter failure while staying in-region. An availability set protects within one datacenter; backups do not keep you running; a second region is overkill for this requirement.
options: Spread the tier across availability zones behind a load balancer
Put all four VMs in one availability set
Rely on nightly backups
Move everything to a second region and leave the first idle
steps.symptom: Guardrails are in place. The web tier must survive a datacenter outage.

simulations.title: The lift-and-shift that wasn't

simulations.brief: HR wants to pilot an AI model that ranks job applications. Your job: review the pilot for responsible-AI risks before it touches real candidates.
simulations.debrief: You applied the responsible-AI reflex: question the data, test for fairness, disclose the system. Accuracy without fairness is a liability, not a feature.

evidence:
Accuracy: 95% (vendor test set, composition undisclosed)
Training data: 'historical hiring decisions, 2015-2023'
steps.explain: Accuracy on an undisclosed test set proves nothing about fairness. Training on historical hiring decisions risks baking past bias into the model — the first responsible-AI question is always: what did this model learn, and from whom?
options: Ask what the test set looks like and whether historical decisions were fair
Accept 95% — accuracy is accuracy
Deploy quietly and watch for complaints
Tune the threshold until every candidate passes
steps.symptom: The vendor demo shows 95% accuracy on their test set. HR is ready to sign.

evidence:
Feature importance: zip_code 0.31, college 0.22
Approval rate gap: 34 points between groups
steps.explain: A 34-point approval gap is a fairness failure, not a tuning detail. Responsible AI requires halting deployment, disclosing the finding, and remediating — removing one column rarely fixes proxy bias, and hiding scores hides accountability.
options: Halt the pilot, disclose the findings, and require bias remediation before any deployment
Ship it — the model is just reflecting reality
Delete the ZIP code column and call it fixed
Keep the pilot but hide the scores from HR
steps.symptom: Your audit finds the model downgrades resumes from certain ZIP codes and women's colleges.

evidence: Current plan: no mention of AI in the application process.
steps.explain: Transparency is a core responsible-AI principle: people affected by an AI system should know it exists and how to contest it. False claims of human review and silence-until-asked both fail that bar.
options: Disclose AI use to candidates and document the system in a transparency note
Say nothing — disclosure invites lawsuits
Claim a human reviews every decision (they do not)
Only disclose if a candidate asks
steps.symptom: Leadership asks how candidates will know an AI screened them.

simulations.title: The resume screener

simulations.brief: An impossible-travel alert fires: a finance user's account signed in from two countries six minutes apart. You have Entra sign-in logs, and the risky-sign-in Conditional Access policy is in report-only mode.
simulations.debrief: You ran the identity incident loop: verify the signal, contain the session, follow the IR plan, then close the gap with enforced Conditional Access and stronger MFA.

evidence:
02:11 EST  Columbus, OH   Success (MFA: SMS)
02:17 EST  Lagos, NG      Success (MFA: SMS)
Device: unrecognized, both sessions
steps.explain: Impossible travel plus an unrecognized device is the textbook account-takeover signal — and SMS MFA is phishable. Verify before assuming: revoke the sessions and require re-authentication now. You can apologize to a traveler, but you cannot un-exfiltrate data.
options: Treat the overseas session as compromised: revoke sessions and force re-authentication
Assume the user is traveling and close the alert
Wait for the user to report a problem
Block the entire country in the firewall
steps.symptom: Alert: finance-02 signed in from Ohio and then from overseas 6 minutes apart.

evidence:
SharePoint: Finance-Q3.xlsx, Payroll-Export.csv, Vendor-Wires.xlsx
Downloaded 02:14–02:16 EST by finance-02 (overseas session)
steps.explain: Containment is not the end — data may have left. Follow the incident response plan: preserve evidence, assess what was taken, and notify the right people in the right order. Company-wide emails and silent hope both make it worse.
options: Start incident response: contain, preserve logs, notify per the IR plan
Delete the files and hope they were not copied
Email the whole company about the breach immediately
Do nothing — the session is revoked
steps.symptom: The overseas session accessed finance SharePoint and downloaded three files before you revoked it.

evidence:
Policy 'Block risky sign-ins': report-only mode
MFA method: SMS for 80% of users
steps.explain: Report-only policies protect no one — enforce the risky-sign-in block and replace phishable SMS MFA with phishing-resistant methods. Zero Trust means verifying every sign-in by risk, not trusting the network or the password.
options: Enforce the risky-sign-in policy and move users to phishing-resistant MFA
Keep report-only — enforcement might annoy travelers
Ban all travel
Require password changes every 30 days
steps.symptom: The account is secured. Leadership asks: how do we stop the next one?
